title: Regression trees: predicting numbers with leaves
intro: A regression tree is the same decision tree as for classification — but every leaf now predicts a number: the mean of the training values in that leaf. The result is a step function you can drag yourself below: move the split points, adjust the leaf means and watch the MSE drop live.
keyPoints: Same tree, different leaf: a classification leaf predicts the majority class, a regression leaf the mean \( c_m \) of the targets in that leaf.
A split minimises the weighted MSE of the children — the regression counterpart of Gini/entropy.
The prediction is a step function: constant per leaf, jumping at the split points — never a slope.
Deeper tree = finer steps = more detail but also more noise; and outside the training range a tree cannot extrapolate.

blocks.html: In the topic Decision trees the tree sorted samples until every leaf was a class. For regression the questions stay the same (“is the floor area below 60 m²?”), but the leaves do something different: they predict a number. Which number? The mean of the target values of the training samples that ended up in that leaf.

That sounds simple — and it is. It is literally the best constant prediction for a fixed group of samples in the least-squares sense: if you want to minimise MSE over a fixed group, you cannot do better than the mean (see the topic Metrics for regression). So the tree only has to search where the boundaries between the groups lie; what to predict inside each group it already knows.

sections.title: Splitting on MSE: the leaf is always the mean

blocks.html: For splitting you need two formulas. One for what a leaf predicts — the mean — and one for what a split costs: the weighted average MSE of the two children:

blocks.label: leaf prediction
blocks.caption: Every leaf m predicts the mean of the n_m target values in it — the constant with the lowest MSE.

blocks.label: split cost
blocks.caption: The weighted MSE of the two children after splitting on feature j at threshold t. The tree picks the (j, t) with the lowest cost.

blocks.html: Worked out on twelve apartments (floor area in m², price in thousand euro). One split at area ≤ 60: the left child catches the four small flats (prices 178, 190, 172, 185), mean \( c_L = 181{,}25 \) with \( \text{MSE}_L = 46{,}7 \). The right child catches the eight larger ones (255 … 341), mean \( c_R = 289 \) with \( \text{MSE}_R = 1995 \) — still a mess, because that group mixes medium and large. The cost of this first split: \( \tfrac{4}{12} \cdot 46{,}7 + \tfrac{8}{12} \cdot 1995 \approx 1346 \).

So the tree splits the right child once more, at area ≤ 90: the medium ones get leaf mean 259 (MSE 37.5), the large ones 344 (MSE 27.5). The tree cost drops to \( \tfrac{4}{12} \cdot 46{,}7 + \tfrac{4}{12} \cdot 37{,}5 + \tfrac{4}{12} \cdot 27{,}5 \approx 37{,}2 \) — a factor 36 better. This is exactly why trees work recursively: every split makes at least one child cleaner, and the tree keeps biting until the brakes (depth, min_samples_leaf) intervene.

Compare this with Gradient descent: linear models approach their optimum with small steps through parameter space. A tree searches its structure with greedy splits — always the best split now, never looking back. The optimisation is very different, but the brake-at-the-end (regularisation vs. pruning) plays exactly the same bias-variance role in both.

Below are the same twelve apartments. The cyan staircase is the tree prediction with two split points (\( t_1, t_2 \)) and three leaf means (\( m_1, m_2, m_3 \)). Drag the sliders to the values from the worked example — \( t_1 = 60 \), \( t_2 = 90 \), \( m_1 = 181 \), \( m_2 = 259 \), \( m_3 = 344 \) — and watch the MSE chip light up green:

blocks.title: Tree with two splits: fit the staircase yourself
blocks.subtitle: Put the split points on the jumps in the data and the leaf means on the levels — the MSE drops live and lights up green at the best fit (37.2).

metrics.label: MSE (k€)²
metrics.expr: pts.reduce((s,p)=>s+((p.x < t1 ? m1 : (p.x < t2 ? m2 : m3))-p.y)**2,0)/pts.length

blocks.html: What you see here is the core of regression trees: the prediction is constant per leaf. Not a slope like linear regression — a series of plateaus. For data that itself thinks in jumps (housing types, tax brackets, threshold subsidies) that fits better than a straight line; for smooth processes (temperature, growth) the line is usually more natural.

Also try what happens when you push \( t_1 \) and \( t_2 \) close together: you create a narrow, thinly populated leaf. The MSE on these twelve points can even drop (parking an outlier in its own leaf), while the prediction on new data becomes arbitrary — the interactive version of overfitting, and exactly why min_samples_leaf exists.

sections.title: Depth, smoothness and the edge of the world

blocks.html: More depth means more steps. With max_depth=1 the tree fits a single jump — too coarse for three housing types (high bias). With unlimited depth every apartment eventually gets its own plateau: perfect on the training set, arbitrary on new data (high variance). The logic is identical to the classification topic: max_depth and min_samples_leaf determine how fine the staircase is, and with it where you sit on the bias-variance axis.

There is one more hard ceiling specific to regression trees: no extrapolation. The model only knows leaf means from the training data — ask for the price of 200 m² and the tree answers with the highest leaf mean it knows (here 344). A linear regression with a positive slope happily projects on to 600; the tree effectively refuses any statement beyond the seen range. Sometimes a flaw, sometimes a virtue: at least it invents nothing.

Rules of thumb: if the underlying relation suits a straight line (or a smooth curve), linear regression is usually more accurate per parameter. If the data itself jumps in thresholds, the tree wins. And never predict far outside the training range with a regression tree — every leaf value is a closed, historical average, not a trend.

The same API as always — the model is just called DecisionTreeRegressor now. The example trains the tree on the twelve apartments from the interactive plot, compares three depths and checks the extrapolation:

blocks.caption: regression tree on the apartment data
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

X = np.array([[36],[42],[48],[55],[63],[70],[78],[85],
               [93],[100],[107],[114]])   # floor area (m2)
y = np.array([178,190,172,185,255,268,252,261,
              345,338,352,341])          # price (kEUR)

for depth in (1, 2, None):
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth,
                                 random_state=0).fit(X, y)
    print('max_depth =', str(depth), '→ R2 train:',
          round(tree.score(X, y), 3),
          '| leaves:', tree.get_n_leaves())

tree2 = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=2,
                              random_state=0).fit(X, y)
for m2 in (50, 75, 100):
    print(m2, 'm2 →', tree2.predict([[m2]])[0], 'kEUR')

# extrapolation: outside the training range the tree
# simply repeats its highest leaf mean
print('200 m2 →', tree2.predict([[200]])[0], 'kEUR (no trend!)')

blocks.html: Note the three lines of output: max_depth=2 already scores almost as well as the unlimited tree on this data, with four leaves instead of twelve. And the prediction for 200 m² is identical to that for 114 m² — the tree cannot go beyond its highest leaf. That is not a bug but architecture: leaf means are constants, not formulas.

For regression too, scikit-learn scans all (feature, threshold) pairs per split. With \( d \) features and \( n \) samples that is \( O(d \cdot n \log n) \) per node — noticeably faster than an SVM kernel on the same data. That, plus scale-independence, makes trees the natural first candidate for tabular regression problems.
